extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funding (school administrators, Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel), policymakers, and practitioners implementing Title IX pregnancy-related provisions
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements under Title IX for how educational recipients must treat students who are pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions, including voluntary separate programs, reasonable modifications, voluntary leaves of absence, verification of medically necessary leave, and lactation space provisions. Focus is on operational compliance and nondiscriminatory treatment across elementary, secondary, and postsecondary settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary participation in separate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient does not engage in prohibited discrimination when it allows a student who is pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions to voluntarily participate in a separate portion of its education program or activity; participation must be completely voluntary and recipients must not coerce or pressure students to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarifies that ‘voluntarily’ means recipients must not coerce or pressure any student into participation. This follows longstanding Title IX interpretation (since 1975) and OCR guidance (1991, 2013 Pregnancy Pamphlets). Suggested alternate constructions to further define or prohibit forcing participation were deemed unnecessary because the existing voluntary standard and anti-coercion interpretation address commenters' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability standard for separate programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate programs available to pregnant or pregnancy-related students must be ‘comparable’ to programs offered to students who are not pregnant and do not have related conditions; ‘comparable’ is understood to mean of equivalent quality or similar such that it is capable of comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable refers to all aspects of a student's access to educational opportunity. An alternative that offers only a vocational track with no advanced or college-preparatory classes would not meet comparability. The Department declined to replace ‘comparable’ with ‘substantially equal’ to avoid implying permissibility limits on legitimate, nondiscriminatory temporary program differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for assessing comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether a separate portion of a program is ‘comparable,’ the Department will consider appropriate factors such as policies and criteria of admission; educational benefits provided (quality, range, and content of curriculum and other services); quality and availability of books, instructional materials, and technology; qualifications of instructors; and quality, accessibility, and availability of facilities and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes §106.34(b)(3) single-sex class factors are relevant and helpful but did not incorporate them verbatim to avoid implying all separate portions are single-sex. Application is fact-specific and depends on the program and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate nondiscriminatory differences allowed for temporary programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary or supplemental programs for pregnant students that differ from permanent academic programs may still be permissible if nondiscriminatory and provide a comparable alternative (e.g., online instruction for a student confined to bed rest or parenting classes that exceed general curriculum offerings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination depends on facts and circumstances; shifting to a ‘substantially equal’ standard could exclude otherwise acceptable supplemental offerings. Examples illustrate when non-identical offerings can still be comparable and permitted under the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to offer reasonable modifications (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have an independent obligation under §106.40(b)(3)(ii) to consult with the student and offer and implement reasonable modifications that meet the student's individualized needs to prevent sex discrimination and ensure equal access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a student's needs exceed what leave provides, or if additional time is needed beyond medically necessary leave, the recipient should consider the request under the reasonable modification standard. Fundamental-alteration inquiries relate to reasonable modifications and not to the obligation to provide voluntary leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary leave of absence — minimum medically necessary period
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must allow a student to take a voluntary leave of absence related to pregnancy or related conditions for, at a minimum, the period of time deemed medically necessary by the student's healthcare provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave must be voluntary. The medically necessary period is a minimum—if the recipient's student leave policy allows a greater period and the student qualifies under that policy, the recipient must permit leave under that longer policy if the student chooses. The Department will not further define ‘academic status’ or ‘leave of absence’ in the regulation; reinstatement requires meaningful opportunity and reasonable time to make up missed coursework or exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement to same academic status after leave
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon return from a voluntary medically necessary leave of absence for pregnancy or related conditions, the recipient must reinstate the student to the same academic status the student held when leave began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstatement includes giving the opportunity to make up missed work; recipients may offer alternatives to making up missed work, especially after longer leaves. There is a presumption of reinstatement to same extracurricular status, though limited administrative impossibility (e.g., activity ended while the student was on leave) may make exact reinstatement impracticable. Specific situations (e.g., student-athletes) are fact-specific and evaluated case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: No worse treatment than other temporary medical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not adopt or apply a medical leave policy that treats a student who withdraws from school due to pregnancy or related conditions worse than a student who withdraws due to any other temporary medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is consistent with §106.40(b)(4) and longstanding Title IX interpretation. The recipient’s policies must treat pregnancy-related conditions the same as other temporary medical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to admitted students prior to start of classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitted (not-yet-enrolled) students qualify for voluntary leave under §106.40(b)(3)(iv); a recipient may not require an admitted student who needs medically necessary leave before classes start or in the first weeks to withdraw and reapply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient has a general policy requiring withdrawal/reapplication for pre-term leave, pregnant students must be exempted to comply with §106.40(b)(3)(iv). If leave exceeds medically necessary period, evaluate as a reasonable modification per §106.40(b)(3)(ii). This applies across elementary/secondary/postsecondary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with Title IV financial aid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient’s Title IX obligation to provide voluntary leave for pregnancy does not necessarily require the recipient to meet Title IV obligations in a manner that disadvantages the student; a pregnancy-related approved leave may also qualify as an approved leave for Title IV purposes depending on 34 CFR 668.22(d)(1)(i)-(viii) factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a leave meets Title IV approved leave criteria, it is a temporary interruption and not a withdrawal for Title IV purposes (no ‘return to Title IV’ calculation). If combined approved leaves exceed 180 days in a 12-month period, the recipient must calculate earned/unearned Title IV funds per 34 CFR 668.22. Recipients may maintain refund policies consistent with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion vs. fundamental alteration for leave
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has discretion in how it administers voluntary leaves of absence as long as implementation is consistent with §106.40(b)(3)(iv), Title IX, and the part; whether leave would fundamentally alter a program is not a basis to deny the basic right to voluntary medically necessary leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental-alteration analysis is relevant to reasonable modifications, not to the requirement to provide leave. The obligation to allow medically necessary leave and reinstate the student has been part of Title IX since 1975 and must be honored regardless of a recipient's view that reinstatement would fundamentally alter the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of medically necessary leave — verifier qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensed healthcare provider may verify that a leave is medically necessary; ‘licensed’ is broadly construed to encompass any healthcare professional qualified to practice in their State and need not be limited to physicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognizes contemporary medical practice (nurse practitioners, midwives, doulas, registered nurses, lactation consultants, etc.) and access issues. Recipients are not required to verify licensure or navigate differing State licensure regimes for various professions; the Department will not require recipients to understand or verify varying licensure requirements across States.

rubrics_metrics.name: When additional leave is needed beyond medically necessary period
rubrics_metrics.description: If a student needs additional time beyond the period deemed medically necessary by their healthcare provider, the recipient should consider the request under the reasonable modification standard of §106.40(b)(3)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application is fact-specific; reasonable modification analysis includes consideration of undue burden/fundamental alteration where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lactation space requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must provide a private, clean, usable lactation space and breaks for a student who is lactating; the space must be suitable for breastfeeding and pumping and should not be a bathroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department found lactation space provision supports health, prevents students from resorting to unsuitable locations (cars, janitor closets, bathroom stalls), and helps maintain access to education. The requirement is consistent with other federal/state laws (e.g., ACA, FLSA) and public health recommendations; commenters requested features like chair, flat surface, electrical outlet, running water, refrigerator/cooler, reasonable proximity, number of spaces, and access during evenings/weekends — the Department recognized these practical concerns though did not mandate each specific feature in the regulation text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and practical considerations for lactation spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may need flexibility in how they comply with the lactation-space requirement (e.g., small schools with limited space); questions include where lactation spaces must be located, required number based on factors, whether construction of new spaces is necessary, and how to administrate shared use when multiple students need access simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department acknowledged commenters' concerns and practicalities; implementation should ensure privacy, hygiene, and usability. The Department also noted some commenters advocated for a right to express milk or breastfeed outside designated lactation spaces consistent with state/local laws that allow breastfeeding in any public place, and the Department considered these perspectives.
